title: George MacDonald
hook: a Scottish storyteller of God's relentless, fatherly love

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chesterton's fairyland: the plain world, as strange and chosen as any story. Your line was the world is strange. What ordinary thing made you look twice? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

A young princess climbs a stair in her own castle she's never noticed before, and at the top finds a room with an old, beautiful woman in it, spinning. The woman says she's the princess's great-great-grandmother. Her nurse doesn't believe a word of it. Later, the grandmother gives the girl a thread so fine she can hardly see it, and tells her to follow it whenever she's afraid. Deep in the dark, under the mountain, the thread leads exactly where she needs to go. That's from The Princess and the Goblin, by George MacDonald, a Scottish minister who became a storyteller. And that thread is a good way into everything he believed about God. Today, George MacDonald.

For MacDonald, God's love was like that thread: hard to see, and impossible to break. He called God Father, and he meant it at full strength. A good father doesn't stop loving a child who runs off. He keeps going after them. MacDonald heard that in Jesus's story of the son who wastes everything and turns for home, where the father sees him "when he was yet a great way off," and runs. In his Unspoken Sermons, MacDonald takes on a line from Hebrews that can sound frightening: "For our God is a consuming fire." Some readers hear a threat. MacDonald heard love. The fire, he said, burns against everything in us that isn't love, our selfishness, our lies, our hardness, and it won't stop burning until those are gone. But it never burns against us. It's the fire of a love that refuses to give up on what it loves. That's what relentless means here: not harsh, but tireless. Some Christians found MacDonald too hopeful. He was willing to hope that this love might reach everyone in the end, and others pushed back on that, and still do. His admirers say he made God's fatherhood feel like coming home. Either way, he told it through fairy tales: goblins and mountains, a North Wind, a princess with a thread. He seems to have trusted that a child, or a grown-up who'd forgotten how to be one, might understand love through a story before they ever followed an argument.
screen: `A THREAD, AND A FATHER` · `HE RUNS TO MEET THE SON` · `A CONSUMING FIRE OF LOVE` · `TOLD THROUGH FAIRY TALES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, in two parts. For now, settle, and breathe. Bring back a story you loved as a child: a fairy tale, a picture book, one somebody read to you at night. Find the moment when someone was lost, or in danger, and help came. Who came? What did it feel like, back then, to hear that part? Sit with that scene for a while. Then, later today, find a fairy tale and read it, MacDonald's or any other, slowly, the way you'd read to a child. If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever first read to you. The bell holds the time.
George MacDonald. The Scottish minister and storyteller who pictured God's love as a father's fire that never lets go.

Your line: love will not let go. Today, think of one person you've stopped expecting much from, and do one small thing that says you haven't given up on them. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians who read George MacDonald often read his fairy tales and his Unspoken Sermons side by side, and some families read his children's books aloud together.

fork.setup: you're the father in Jesus's story. your son wasted everything, and now he's on the road home, still a great way off. what do you do?
options: wait at the door to hear his apology.
send a servant to ask why he's back.
fork.reveal: Luke 15:20: the father "saw him, and had compassion, and ran." MacDonald heard God's fatherly love in that run.

original.note: Greek, Hebrews 12:29: a consuming fire — which MacDonald read as the fire of love.

notes: Hook retells The Princess and the Goblin (Irene, her great-great-grandmother spinning, the nearly invisible thread tied to a ring); confirm details.
'A Scottish minister who became a storyteller': MacDonald served as a Congregational minister before turning to writing; confirm phrasing.
MacDonald's hope that God's love might reach everyone in the end (often described as Christian universalism) is stated as his hope, with pushback noted; confirm fair and appropriate for this path.
The Consuming Fire sermon is paraphrased; no quotation from MacDonald.
Fork reveal quotes part of Luke 15:20 KJV ('saw him, and had compassion, and ran').
